article.title: Like Benjamin Franklin
article.author: Dimitris Eleas
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Some people make history when they win the presidency; others, like Benjamin Franklin, shaped the nation without ever holding its highest office. Americans have voted on the six years of Donald Trump's era of excess. Four years of his first presidency and two of his second. The November 3 midterm elections offered a glimmer of hope for American democracy. The big question was whether the Democrats would manage to regain control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, putting a check on the president. They succeeded in both chambers ! The results send a message of change. They marked the end of the political careers of many politicians. Trump governed, and continues to govern, with a personal, often imperial style, one eyebrow raised and a glint in his eye, often treating the presidency as if it were his private business. His political presence, somewhere between the excesses of a Hollywood star and the behavior of a Wild West saloon owner, has created deep divisions within society. Under his leadership, America has often looked like a Wild West movie set. But democracy is no one’s spoils. Related: The AI Race Is Accelerating: Who Will Hit the Brakes? The most important issue is people’s everyday lives. The high cost of food, the cost of energy and housing, the uncertainty surrounding healthcare, and ICE’s harsh immigration operations have created an explosive social environment. Thousands of families are living in fear of deportation. The slogan “America First” has devolved into “America First for the Few” – an America that puts the financially powerful and billionaires first. And so, Elon Musk backed the Republicans with $446 million , only to see that money go up in smoke. However, the Republican Party is not the only one responsible for what is happening in America today. The Democrats also bear a significant share of the responsibility. For three decades, to a large extent, they forgot the poor and the working class. They moved away from the real concerns of society and left room for Trump’s populism. You cannot defend democracy if you are indifferent to social justice. I am 100% politically independent. Today, however, I believe that America needs a strong opposition, and fortunately, it will have one. It needs new politicians with social sensitivity, but also the political vision of someone like Senator Bernie Sanders. If he had been given the opportunity to run for president and win in 2016, perhaps America today would be different. Related: Trump Suspends Attack on Iran but Who are the Real Winners and Losers Of course, a politician’s historical importance is not measured by whether he becomes president, but by the ideas he leaves behind and the changes he inspires. Benjamin Franklin never became president, yet secured a permanent place in American history. Perhaps Sanders, in his own way, will do the same. (Actually, many people think Mr. $100 Bill was indeed a president!) He lost the nomination back then because the Democratic Party undermined him in favor of the warmongering Hillary Clinton. The Democratic Party must start talking again about decent wages, public healthcare, and tax fairness. Bernie advocates for Medicare for All and a nationwide minimum wage of $20 an hour. And the party must use even the word socialism wisely, a word that continues to make a large part of American society uncomfortable. The Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and Trump will now face a strong institutional counterweight. He will no longer be able to treat Congress as a mechanism for automatically approving his decisions. But this victory is not a blank check. It requires responsibility, unity, and political maturity on the part of the Democrats. Related: Why Iran War Is Not Going Well for U.S. and Israel We are living through historic moments. America’s Founders, Franklin among them, created institutions precisely to protect democracy from the excessive concentration of power or the emergence of the kind of phenomena we have witnessed over these six years. Today, the Democrats, above all, are called upon to defend them in practice. It is a great country, with weaknesses, contradictions, and enormous potential. The scale of the Republicans’ stunning defeat , however, may, in time, also help heal the wounds left behind by the Trump hurricane as it swept through politics and society. Perhaps the cracks already present within the MAGA movement’s base will grow even wider. But the Party of Reagan, too, will have to wake up from its deep slumber. Even Mitt Romney has called for a “ course correction ” within his party. And some of the political seeds Bernie Sanders planted have finally borne fruit. Several candidates he endorsed won their races, giving the progressive movement a stronger voice in Congress. Sanders’s lasting legacy is his vision of a society for all and a government for the many, not just the few. Electoral victories may be short-lived, but the power of ideas is eternal. Personality is what makes a human being a history-making creature! Franklin left his mark without becoming president. Sanders has achieved something similar in our time. And who knows? If America one day introduces a $200 bill, the Wise and Independent Man of Vermont may appear on it. He would certainly deserve it.
